bottleneck: Reprogramming somatic cells into iPSCs and expanding them in culture introduces copy-number variants, point mutations, and epigenetic abnormalities. Some aberrations affect oncogenes or tumor suppressors, raising the specter of graft-derived tumors years after transplantation. Screening every line deeply is possible but expensive, and the long-term significance of many variants is unknown, leaving developers to guess which abnormalities are acceptable. Culture adaptation itself selects for growth-advantaged, potentially dangerous variants.
current_state: Non-integrating reprogramming and improved culture reduce but do not eliminate abnormalities. Clinical iPSC programs bank and extensively characterize lines, accepting the considerable cost and delay.

title: iPSC reprogramming introduces genomic instability
why_it_blocks: A regenerative cell that might turn cancerous is not a therapy. Genomic instability forces costly screening and long follow-up, slowing iPSC medicine to a crawl while patients wait for grafts.
